comment: The text states that consent is the primary mechanism by which individuals exercise control over their health data. This conflates consent, legal basis, authorization and data rights. Public-health surveillance and many care operations may rely on statutory or public-interest bases; consent may not be freely given or operationally appropriate. Conversely, a lawful basis does not remove duties of transparency, minimization, security, correction and redress. WHO’s data principles similarly distinguish ethical data governance from blanket openness or consent: https://www.who.int/data/principles/

public.text: The text states that consent is the primary mechanism by which individuals exercise control over their health data. This conflates consent, legal basis, authorization and data rights. Public-health surveillance and many care operations may rely on statutory or public-interest bases; consent may not be freely given or operationally appropriate. Conversely, a lawful basis does not remove duties of transparency, minimization, security, correction and redress. WHO’s data principles similarly distinguish ethical data governance from blanket openness or consent: https://www.who.int/data/principles/
public.suggestedRevision:
Distinguish: (1) lawful basis for processing; (2) authorization and role-based access; (3) consent where consent is appropriate; and (4) enforceable individual/community rights. Require purpose limitation, minimization, access logs, correction, appeal/redress, independent oversight and special safeguards for surveillance and vulnerable populations.

If limited by space, acknowledge that consent policies vary not only at the level of "systems that hold and exchange the data" but also within a system itself (e.g. public health surveillance may have different consent policies depending on type of disease or population). Consent resouces should contain at a minimum lawful basis, consent tupe, authorization and acces.
